constraints: l != b and b != h and l != h
families.stem: A rectangular prism has length {=l} cm, breadth {=b} cm and height {=h} cm. Calculate its total surface area, that is, the area of all six faces. Give your answer in cm$^2$.
solution: A rectangular prism has six rectangular faces. Its net is made up of three pairs of equal rectangles: the top and bottom, the front and back, and the two sides. Find the area of each face and add them together.
Top and bottom: each face is {=l} cm by {=b} cm, so their total area is $2 \times ({=l} \times {=b}) = 2 \times {=top} = {=2 * top}$ cm$^2$.
Front and back: each face is {=l} cm by {=h} cm, so their total area is $2 \times ({=l} \times {=h}) = 2 \times {=front} = {=2 * front}$ cm$^2$.
Two sides: each face is {=b} cm by {=h} cm, so their total area is $2 \times ({=b} \times {=h}) = 2 \times {=side} = {=2 * side}$ cm$^2$.
Add the areas of all six faces: ${=2 * top} + {=2 * front} + {=2 * side} = {=total}$ cm$^2$. The surface area is {=total} cm$^2$.
families.notes: Basic entry point of the objective: a plain rectangular prism with all three dimensions given in the stem (no figure needed, so the stem stands alone). Modelled on book question ex13-7-4 (p. 458), which also gives the dimensions in words and finds the area of each face and adds; this family keeps the three dimensions different so the net really has three different pairs of rectangles, and the solution shows each pair separately. The stem says 'total surface area, all six faces' so a blind solver cannot read it as an open box. Dimensions are whole cm, bounded 6-12, 3-8 and 2-9, so the answer is a whole number of cm^2 between 2*(18+12+6)=72ish and 552; no rounding is involved. No distractors, so no misconception ids are used (none are catalogued for this objective). The standard and advanced tiers already exist in the bank from the book questions and were not asked for here.

families.stem: A cylinder has a radius of ${=r}$ $\text{cm}$ and a height of ${=h}$ $\text{cm}$. Its curved surface unfolds into a rectangle: one side of the rectangle is the height of the cylinder and the other side is the circumference of the base. Find the area of the curved surface only (not the two circular ends). Use the $\pi$ button on your calculator and round your answer to 1 decimal place, in $\text{cm}^{2}$.
solution: When the curved surface is unrolled it forms a rectangle. One side is the height of the cylinder, ${=h}$ $\text{cm}$. The other side went once round the base, so its length is the circumference of the base circle.
Circumference of the base: $2\pi r=2\pi({=r})={=2*r}\pi$ $\text{cm}$.
Area of the curved surface = length $\times$ height: $A=({=2*r}\pi)\times({=h})={=2*r*h}\pi$ $\text{cm}^{2}$.
Use the $\pi$ button on your calculator and round to 1 decimal place: ${=2*r*h}\pi\approx{=fixed(2*pi*r*h, 1)}$ $\text{cm}^{2}$.
families.notes: Entry point of the skill: the curved surface alone, i.e. the book's rectangle step (rectangle length = circumference of the base, width = height), with no circles to add yet. Same step as the 'b(2*pi*r)' line of ex13-7-5 and the 'area of larger rectangle' line of we04. Radius is always given, never the diameter. The solution keeps everything in terms of pi until the last line, so no intermediate rounding appears in any step. Rounding guard: the tenths fraction is kept more than 0.1 away from 0.5, so a solver using pi to 4 decimals (3.1416) still prints the same 1 d.p. value; 160 of the 198 (r,h) pairs pass. Spot-check against the book: r=6,h=11 gives 132*pi = 414.7, consistent with the book's ex13-7-5 total of 204*pi = 640.88 once the two circles (72*pi) are added. No distractors, so no misconception ids are used.

families.stem: A closed cylinder is cut open and flattened into a net made of two identical circles and one rectangle. The rectangle measures ${=2*r}\pi$ $\text{cm}$ by ${=h}$ $\text{cm}$, and its ${=2*r}\pi$ $\text{cm}$ side is the part that went right round the base of the cylinder. Find the total surface area of the cylinder. Use the $\pi$ button on your calculator and give your answer correct to 1 decimal place, in $\text{cm}^{2}$.
solution: The ${=2*r}\pi$ $\text{cm}$ side of the rectangle went once round the base, so it equals the circumference of the base circle: $2\pi r={=2*r}\pi$.
Divide both sides by $2\pi$ to find the radius of the circles: $r={=r}$ $\text{cm}$.
Area of the rectangle (the curved surface) $=({=2*r}\pi)\times({=h})={=2*r*h}\pi$ $\text{cm}^{2}$.
Area of the two circular ends $=2\pi r^{2}=2\pi({=r})^{2}={=2*r*r}\pi$ $\text{cm}^{2}$.
Surface area = rectangle + two circles $={=2*r*h}\pi+{=2*r*r}\pi={=2*r*(r+h)}\pi\approx{=fixed(2*pi*r*(r+h), 1)}$ $\text{cm}^{2}$.
families.notes: Advanced twist: the net is described by its rectangle only, and the circles' radius is not given. The student must use the book's own key fact (the rectangle's length is the circumference of the base) in reverse, 2*pi*r = length, to recover r, then add the rectangle and the two circles as in we04. The length is given in terms of pi (2r*pi) so r is an exact whole number and no intermediate rounding can make solvers disagree. The stem says which side wrapped round the base, so the height cannot be confused with the circumference even when h exceeds 2*pi*r (e.g. r=3, h=20). Check against the book: r=10, h=30 gives 2*pi*10*40 = 800*pi = 2513.3, matching we04. Same rounding guard as the basic family; 130 of the 170 (r,h) pairs pass; answers range from about 150.8 to 2142.6. No distractors, so no misconception ids are used.

records.notes: Two numeric families for the two gap tiers, both within the book's own method (net = two circles + a rectangle whose length is the circumference). Basic = the curved surface alone (the rectangle step). Advanced = total surface area from a net whose rectangle length is given as 2*r*pi, so the radius must be recovered. The standard tier is not written: the two book questions already sit there. No misconceptions are catalogued for this objective and none are proposed, since both families are numeric with no distractors. Both solutions stay in exact multiples of pi until the final line and the params guard against rounding-boundary answers. Both figures of the book questions were viewed before writing.

families.stem: The volume of a cylinder is the area of its circular base multiplied by its height. A cylinder has a radius of ${=r}$ cm and a height of ${=h}$ cm. Calculate the volume of the cylinder in $\text{cm}^3$, correct to 1 decimal place. Use the $\pi$ button on your calculator.
solution: Find the area of the circular base: $\text{area of base} = \pi r^{2} = \pi({=r})^{2} = {=r * r}\pi \text{ cm}^{2}$
Multiply the area of the base by the height of the cylinder: $V = \text{area of base} \times \text{height} = {=r * r}\pi \times {=h} = {=r * r * h}\pi \text{ cm}^{3}$
Use the $\pi$ button on your calculator and round to 1 decimal place: $V = {=r * r * h}\pi \approx {=fixed(pi * r ** 2 * h, 1)} \text{ cm}^{3}$
Write the final answer: the volume of the cylinder is ${=fixed(pi * r ** 2 * h, 1)}$ $\text{cm}^{3}$.
families.notes: Entry point of the skill, modelled on book worked example 7 (r = 4 cm, h = 15 cm, 1 d.p.; figure seen, radius labelled, height labelled). The figure cannot be sampled, so the stem gives both measurements in words. The stem states the book's own definition (area of base x height) as a scaffold; the solution follows the book's two steps exactly (base area, then multiply by the height). r is 2 to 6 and h is 3 to 12 (never equal to r), so volumes run from about 38 to 1357 cm^3 (40 clean instances). A require keeps the volume at least 0.1 of a unit in the first decimal place away from a rounding tie, so a solver using the calculator's pi (or 3.14159) gets the same rounded answer. The stem tells the student to use the pi button; an answer worked with 3.14 is not intended to be accepted. Numeric answer is unitless (cm^3 is stated in the stem). No mcq: the misconception list for this objective is empty.

families.stem: A cylinder has a diameter of ${=d}$ cm and a height of ${=hs}$ cm. Calculate the volume of the cylinder in $\text{cm}^3$, correct to 2 decimal places. Use the $\pi$ button on your calculator and do not round until your final answer.
solution: The formula uses the radius, so first halve the diameter: $r = {=d} \div 2 = {=rs}$ cm
Find the area of the circular base: $\text{area of base} = \pi r^{2} = \pi({=rs})^{2} = {=rsq}\pi \text{ cm}^{2}$
Multiply the area of the base by the height of the cylinder: $V = \text{area of base} \times \text{height} = {=rsq}\pi \times {=hs} = {=vp}\pi \text{ cm}^{3}$
Use the $\pi$ button on your calculator and round to 2 decimal places: $V = {=vp}\pi \approx {=fixed(pi * m / 8, 2)} \text{ cm}^{3}$
Write the final answer: the volume of the cylinder is ${=fixed(pi * m / 8, 2)}$ $\text{cm}^{3}$.
families.notes: Advanced tier. Same book method as ex13-7-8 (r = 7 cm, h = 12 cm, 2 d.p.; figure seen, radius labelled, height labelled) and we07, with two added twists: the DIAMETER is given, so the radius must be found by halving first (odd diameters give a radius ending in .5, for example d = 9 gives r = 4.5 and r^2 = 20.25), and the height is a half-integer such as 12.5 cm. Rounding is to 2 d.p., as in ex13-7-8. d is 5 to 14 and the height is 4.5 to 18.5 cm, so volumes run from about 88 to 2848 cm^3 (122 clean instances). Worked-step numbers are built as exact strings: rsq is r^2 (an integer or x.25), vp is r^2 x h (0, 1 or 3 decimals, exactly m/8 with m = d^2 x (2*hh+1)), and the final value is pi*m/8. A require keeps the volume at least 0.1 of a unit in the second decimal place away from a rounding tie, so a solver using the calculator's pi (or 3.14159) gets the same rounded answer. The stem tells the student to use the pi button and not to round early; an answer worked with 3.14 is not intended to be accepted. Numeric answer is unitless (cm^3 is stated in the stem). No mcq: the misconception list for this objective is empty, and a worked numeric answer is the natural response.

records.notes: Two families written, one per listed gap (basic and advanced). A standard family was not written because standard was not listed as a gap and the three book questions of this objective (we07, ex13-3-6, ex13-7-8) are already the standard exercises; a third family would only repeat the basic skeleton with larger numbers. All three book figures were read: each shows a plain cylinder with the radius and the height labelled in cm, so both families state the measurements in words. The misconception list for this objective is empty, so neither family is an mcq and no misconception ids are used or declared. Both families are numeric, use the calculator's pi key, and are guarded by a require that keeps the exact volume clear of a rounding tie. I could not run the family engine here (only the packet files may be opened), so the expression forms (fixed on exact fractions, str, //, conditional let params, floor/abs/pi in a require) are unverified against it; I checked the sampled ranges, instance counts, margins and the example values in plain Python (for example r=4, h=11 gives 552.9; d=9, h=12.5 gives vp=253.125 and 795.22).

families.stem: A pyramid has a square base with sides of ${=b}$ cm. Its four triangular faces are identical, and each has a slant height of ${=s}$ cm (the height of the triangle, measured up the face from the middle of a base edge to the apex). Calculate the total surface area of the pyramid in $\text{cm}^{2}$.
solution: The surface of the pyramid is the square base together with four identical triangular faces, so $\text{surface area}=\text{area of base}+4\times\text{area of one triangular face}$.
Area of the base: $b^{2}={=b}^{2}={=b*b}\text{ cm}^{2}$.

Each triangular face has base ${=b}$ cm and height equal to the slant height ${=s}$ cm, so the four faces together have area $4\times\frac{1}{2}\times b\times h_s=4\times\frac{1}{2}\times{=b}\times{=s}={=2*b*s}\text{ cm}^{2}$.
Add the areas: $\text{surface area}={=b*b}+{=2*b*s}={=b*b+2*b*s}\text{ cm}^{2}$.
families.notes: Entry point of the skill, modelled on ex13-7-10 and ex13-4-4: square base plus four triangles, with the slant height given and no vertical height to confuse it. Whole numbers throughout; b from 4 to 14, slant height always above half the base so the pyramid exists. Stem defines slant height in words because no figure is available.

params.why: the slant height must be a whole number, so that the working stays clean

families.stem: A pyramid has a square base with sides of ${=b}$ cm. Its vertical height (from the apex straight down to the centre of the base) is ${=h}$ cm, and each of its four identical triangular faces has a slant height of ${=s}$ cm. What is the total surface area of the pyramid?
solution: The surface area is the area of the square base plus the area of the four triangular faces.

The height of each triangular face is the slant height, ${=s}$ cm, because it is measured along the face. The vertical height of ${=h}$ cm runs inside the pyramid and is not the height of a face, so it is not used here.
Area of the base: ${=b}^{2}={=b*b}\text{ cm}^{2}$.
Area of the four faces: $4\times\frac{1}{2}\times{=b}\times{=s}={=2*b*s}\text{ cm}^{2}$.
Total surface area: ${=b*b}+{=2*b*s}={=b*b+2*b*s}\text{ cm}^{2}$.

proposed_misconceptions.label: Base left out of the total surface area
proposed_misconceptions.description: The student adds up only the four triangular faces and forgets the square base, so the answer is 2bh_s instead of b^2 + 2bh_s.

proposed_misconceptions.label: Triangle area without the one half
proposed_misconceptions.description: The student finds the area of each triangular face as base times slant height, leaving out the factor of one half, so the four faces come to 4bh_s instead of 2bh_s.

families.notes: Standard tier, built on the book's own decoy: ex13-4-4 and ex13-7-10 print the vertical height beside the slant height. Every instance satisfies h^2 + (b/2)^2 = s^2 (table of Pythagorean triples, 14 of them, so the printed vertical height is true for the printed slant height). Three distractors, each a named error; all four options are proved distinct for every table row (b+2h = 2s is impossible because (m+h)^2 > m^2+h^2). The mcq earns its place because each distractor is diagnosable, and the existing catalogue id is used on the vertical-height option.

families.stem: A triangular pyramid has a base that is an equilateral triangle with sides of ${=b}$ cm. The apex is directly above the centre of the base, so its three triangular faces are identical, and each has a slant height of ${=s}$ cm (the height of the triangle, measured from the apex at right angles to a base edge). Calculate the total surface area of the pyramid, correct to 1 decimal place, in $\text{cm}^{2}$.
solution: The surface is the equilateral triangle base plus three identical triangular faces, so $\text{surface area}=\text{area of base}+3\times\text{area of one face}$.
To find the area of the base we need its perpendicular height $h_b$. It splits the base into two right-angled triangles, each with hypotenuse ${=b}$ cm and one short side $\frac{{=b}}{2}={=m}$ cm.
By the theorem of Pythagoras: $h_b^{2}={=b}^{2}-{=m}^{2}={=b*b}-{=m*m}={=b*b-m*m}$, so $h_b=\sqrt{{=b*b-m*m}}={=m}\sqrt{3}\approx{=fixed(m*sqrt(3), 3)}$ cm.
Area of the base: $\frac{1}{2}\times b\times h_b=\frac{1}{2}\times{=b}\times{=m}\sqrt{3}={=m*m}\sqrt{3}\approx{=fixed(m*m*sqrt(3), 3)}\text{ cm}^{2}$.
Area of the three faces: $3\times\frac{1}{2}\times b\times h_s=3\times\frac{1}{2}\times{=b}\times{=s}={=3*m*s}\text{ cm}^{2}$.
Add the areas: $\text{surface area}={=m*m}\sqrt{3}+{=3*m*s}\approx{=fixed(m*m*sqrt(3), 3)}+{=3*m*s}\approx{=fixed(X, 3)}$, which is ${=fixed(X, 1)}\text{ cm}^{2}$ correct to 1 decimal place.
families.notes: Modelled on worked example 8 (we08: base 6 cm, face height 10 cm, answer 9*sqrt(3) + 90 = 105.6). The book solution is exact-then-round, which is what this does. The base side is 2m with m in {3, 4, 5} so that half of it is whole and h_b = m*sqrt(3). m = 6 and 8 were left out deliberately: m^2*sqrt(3) lies within 0.005 of a rounding boundary (62.354, 110.851) and a blind solver rounding sqrt(3) early could land on the other side. For m in {3, 4, 5} the unrounded value is at least 0.037 from a boundary, so rounding h_b to 2 or 3 decimal places first gives the same 1-decimal answer (checked: 15.588, 27.713, 43.301 for the base). Answers range from 69.6 to 313.3.

families.stem: A pyramid has a square base with sides of ${=b}$ cm. Its apex is directly above the centre of the base, at a vertical height of ${=h}$ cm. The slant height is not given. Calculate the total surface area of the pyramid in $\text{cm}^{2}$.
solution: The four triangular faces need the slant height $h_s$, which is not given, so find it first. The slant height, the vertical height and half of a base side form a right-angled triangle, with the slant height as the hypotenuse.
Half of the base side: $\frac{{=b}}{2}={=m}$ cm.
By the theorem of Pythagoras: $h_s^{2}={=h}^{2}+{=m}^{2}={=h*h}+{=m*m}={=h*h+m*m}$, so $h_s=\sqrt{{=h*h+m*m}}={=s}$ cm.
Area of the base: ${=b}^{2}={=b*b}\text{ cm}^{2}$.
Area of the four triangular faces: $4\times\frac{1}{2}\times{=b}\times{=s}={=2*b*s}\text{ cm}^{2}$.
Total surface area: $\text{base}+\text{faces}={=b*b}+{=2*b*s}={=b*b+2*b*s}\text{ cm}^{2}$.
families.notes: Advanced: the slant height has to be found first (the book's own twist, ex13-7-29b: AF = sqrt(a^2 + h^2) with a = half of BC), then the total surface area is a second stage. The table gives 14 (half-base, height) pairs whose hypotenuse is a whole number, so every slant height and every answer is a whole number and nothing is rounded (a decimal version would let a solver that rounds the slant height early land on a different 1-decimal answer). Common error to watch for in review: using the full base side instead of half of it in the Pythagoras step.

records.notes: Four families, all numeric except one mcq. Basic (square-slant, parent ex13-7-10): the slant height is given, so the surface area is the base plus four triangles. Advanced (pythagoras-slant, parent ex13-7-29b): the vertical height and base side are given, so the slant height comes from Pythagoras with half the base, then the total area. I added two standard-tier families beyond the listed gaps. The reason is that no families existed at all, and the LO names the triangular pyramid and the vertical-height decoy that both appear in the book. decoy-heights is an mcq on ex13-4-4: every distractor is a named error, and it uses the catalogued id vertical-height-for-slant-height plus two new ones declared in proposed_misconceptions. triangular-base (parent we08) has an equilateral base with Pythagoras for the base height, answer to 1 d.p.; I excluded base sides whose base-triangle area sits within 0.005 of a rounding boundary so blind solvers cannot split on rounding. Slug prefixes are square, decoy-, triang and pythag, so the item ids do not collide. I simulated all four families with a local re-implementation of the template language (not the real engine): all values render, the mcq options are distinct in 300 draws each, and the families yield 113, 14, 27 and 14 distinct stems. The mcq and advanced families have only 14 distinct stems each (the Pythagorean-triple table), which covers ten instances but not by a wide margin. No figures are used: slant and vertical heights are defined in words in each stem, because the book diagrams cannot be reproduced.

families.stem: A right cone has a base radius of ${=r}$ cm and a slant height of ${=h}$ cm. Calculate the total surface area of the cone in cm$^2$, that is, the area of the circular base plus the area of the walls. Use the value of $\pi$ on your calculator and round your answer to 1 decimal place.
solution: The total surface area of a cone is the area of the circular base plus the area of the walls: $\pi r^2 + \pi r h$, where $r$ is the radius and $h$ is the slant height.
Area of the base: $\pi r^2 = \pi \times {=r}^2 = {=r*r}\pi$ cm$^2$.
Area of the walls, using the slant height: $\pi r h = \pi \times {=r} \times {=h} = {=r*h}\pi$ cm$^2$.
Add the two areas: ${=r*r}\pi + {=r*h}\pi = {=r*r + r*h}\pi \approx {=fixed(area, 1)}$ cm$^2$.
The total surface area of the cone is {=fixed(area, 1)} cm$^2$.
families.notes: Entry point of the skill: the slant height is GIVEN, so the student only has to add the base circle and the walls (the book's wording in we09: area of base plus area of walls; ex13-4-2 writes the same sum as pi*r*(r+h)). The book's ex13-4-2 also prints the vertical height as a spare datum; the basic tier leaves it out so only r and h appear. Answer is pi*r*(r+h) rounded to 1 dp, as in we09 and ex13-4-1c; the stem tells the student to use the calculator's pi, and a require drops the instances whose exact value sits within 0.005 of a rounding boundary (about 16 percent of the draws). h runs from r+2 to 16, so h > r always and the cone is geometrically valid. About 64 distinct (r, h) instances survive. Typical wrong answers, for the reviewer: leaving out the base (pi*r*h), or using 2*pi*r*h for the walls.

constraints: hs * hs == r * r + hv * hv
families.stem: A right cone has a base radius of ${=r}$ cm, a vertical height of ${=hv}$ cm and a slant height of ${=hs}$ cm. Which calculation gives the total surface area of the cone, that is, the area of the circular base plus the area of the walls?
solution: The total surface area of the cone is the area of the circular base plus the area of the walls.
The base is a circle of radius ${=r}$ cm, so its area is $\pi r^2 = \pi \times {=r}^2$.

The walls have area $\pi r h$, where $h$ is the slant height, the length along the wall from the apex to the edge of the base. Here that is ${=hs}$ cm, not the vertical height of ${=hv}$ cm: $\pi \times {=r} \times {=hs}$.

Adding the two areas gives $\pi \times {=r}^2 + \pi \times {=r} \times {=hs}$. Leaving out the base, using the vertical height in place of the slant height, or using the cylinder's wall area $2\pi r h$ would each give a different value.

proposed_misconceptions.label: Leaves out the circular base
proposed_misconceptions.description: Gives only the area of the walls, pi*r*h, when asked for the total surface area, which also includes the area of the base circle.

proposed_misconceptions.label: Uses the vertical height for the walls
proposed_misconceptions.description: Puts the vertical height (apex straight down to the centre of the base) into pi*r*h instead of the slant height measured along the wall.

proposed_misconceptions.label: Uses the cylinder's wall area for the cone
proposed_misconceptions.description: Writes the walls as 2*pi*r*h, the curved area of a cylinder, instead of pi*r*h for a cone.

families.notes: A basic recognition item for the formula pi*r^2 + pi*r*h, a natural multiple choice because the point is choosing the right set-up and each distractor is one named error. The stem gives r, the vertical height and the slant height as the same Pythagorean triple (r, vertical height, slant height) so the geometry is real and the vertical-height distractor is tempting; the three distractors are never numerically equal to the correct option because the vertical height differs from the slant height. 15 distinct stems. No distinct_by_choices key needed because the stem holes differ between instances. The catalogue for this objective was empty, so all three ids are new.

families.stem: A right cone has a base radius of ${=r}$ cm and a vertical height of ${=hv}$ cm. Its slant height is not given. Calculate the total surface area of the cone in cm$^2$, that is, the area of the circular base plus the area of the walls. Use the value of $\pi$ on your calculator and round your answer to 1 decimal place.
solution: The slant height $h$ is the hypotenuse of a right-angled triangle whose other two sides are the radius and the vertical height. By the theorem of Pythagoras: $h^2 = r^2 + H^2 = {=r}^2 + {=hv}^2 = {=r*r + hv*hv}$, so $h = {=hs}$ cm.
Area of the base: $\pi r^2 = \pi \times {=r}^2 = {=r*r}\pi$ cm$^2$.
Area of the walls: $\pi r h = \pi \times {=r} \times {=hs} = {=r*hs}\pi$ cm$^2$.
Total surface area = area of the base + area of the walls = ${=r*r}\pi + {=r*hs}\pi = {=r*r + r*hs}\pi \approx {=fixed(area, 1)}$ cm$^2$.
The total surface area of the cone is {=fixed(area, 1)} cm$^2$.
families.notes: Follows the book's we09 (radius and vertical height given, slant height found with the theorem of Pythagoras, then base plus walls, rounded to 1 dp). we09 itself uses r = 4 and H = 14, where the slant height is the surd sqrt(212); here (r, vertical height, slant height) is always a Pythagorean triple so the slant height is a whole number and no solver can drift by rounding it halfway through. The skill is unchanged: the student must still recognise the right-angled triangle formed by the radius, the vertical height and the slant height. Both orientations (radius the shorter or the longer leg) are included so the radius is not always the small number. A require drops draws whose exact answer is within 0.005 of a 1 dp rounding boundary; all 15 table rows survive it (checked), giving 15 distinct instances. Typical wrong answers, for the reviewer: using the vertical height as the slant height (pi*r*(r+H)), or leaving out the base.

families.stem: One sphere has a radius of ${=fixed(a/10, 1)}$ cm and a second sphere has a radius of ${=fixed(b/10, 1)}$ cm. Find the total surface area of the two spheres, in $\text{cm}^{2}$, correct to 1 decimal place. Use the value of $\pi$ on your calculator and round only at the end.
solution: The surface area of a sphere is $A=4\pi r^{2}$. Work out the surface area of each sphere, then add the two areas.
First sphere: $\begin{aligned}A_{1}&=4\pi r^{2}\\&=4\pi({=fixed(a/10, 1)})^{2}\\&={=fixed(4*a*a/100, 2)}\pi\end{aligned}$
Second sphere: $\begin{aligned}A_{2}&=4\pi r^{2}\\&=4\pi({=fixed(b/10, 1)})^{2}\\&={=fixed(4*b*b/100, 2)}\pi\end{aligned}$

Add the two areas, keeping $\pi$ exact until the end: $\begin{aligned}A_{1}+A_{2}&=({=fixed(4*a*a/100, 2)}+{=fixed(4*b*b/100, 2)})\pi\\&={=fixed((4*a*a+4*b*b)/100, 2)}\pi\\&\approx{=fixed(4 * pi * (a * a + b * b) / 100, 1)}\end{aligned}$
Therefore the total surface area of the two spheres is approximately ${=fixed(4 * pi * (a * a + b * b) / 100, 1)}\text{ cm}^{2}$, correct to 1 decimal place.

families.stem: A solid is made by placing a square-based pyramid on top of a cube. The edges of the cube are ${=s}\text{ cm}$ long. The base of the pyramid is exactly the top face of the cube, and the height of the pyramid itself (from its base up to its apex) is ${=H}\text{ cm}$. Calculate the volume of the whole solid, in $\text{cm}^{3}$.
solution: The solid is a cube with a pyramid on top of it, so its volume is the volume of the cube plus the volume of the pyramid.
Volume of the cube: $\begin{aligned}V_{\text{cube}}&=l^{3}\\&=({=s})^{3}\\&={=s**3}\text{ cm}^{3}\end{aligned}$

The base of the pyramid is the top face of the cube, a square with side ${=s}\text{ cm}$. Volume of the pyramid: $\begin{aligned}V_{\text{pyramid}}&=\frac{1}{3}b^{2}H\\&=\frac{1}{3}({=s})^{2}({=H})\\&={=s**2*m}\text{ cm}^{3}\end{aligned}$
Total volume: $\begin{aligned}V_{\text{total}}&=V_{\text{cube}}+V_{\text{pyramid}}\\&={=s**3}+{=s**2*m}\\&={=s**3 + s**2*m}\text{ cm}^{3}\end{aligned}$
Therefore the total volume of the solid is ${=s**3 + s**2*m}\text{ cm}^{3}$.
families.notes: Entry point of the skill: the pyramid's own height is GIVEN, so the student only adds V_cube = s^3 and V_pyramid = (1/3)b^2 H, exactly the book's method in ex13-7-20b (which is advanced because it first asks for H = 22 - 7). H is drawn as 3m so the pyramid volume s^2*m is a whole number and the answer is an integer; m <= s keeps the pyramid no taller than 3 edge lengths. s = 7, m = 5 reproduces the book's 588. The stem is fully worded (no figure) and states that the height is the pyramid's own, so uses-total-height-for-pyramid cannot arise at this tier. The likeliest wrong answer is forgetting the 1/3 (s^3 + s^2*H).

families.stem: A solid is made by placing a square-based pyramid on top of a cube. The edges of the cube are ${=s}\text{ cm}$ long and the base of the pyramid is exactly the top face of the cube. Each triangular face of the pyramid has a slant height of ${=hs}\text{ cm}$ (the height of that triangle, measured from the middle of its base edge up to the apex). Calculate the total surface area of the solid, that is, the area of all the faces on the outside of the solid. Give your answer in $\text{cm}^{2}$.
solution: The top face of the cube is covered by the pyramid, and the base of the pyramid is covered by the cube, so neither is part of the outside of the solid. The exposed faces are the bottom face and the four side faces of the cube (five squares) and the four triangular faces of the pyramid.
Area of the five squares: $\begin{aligned}A_{\text{five squares}}&=5\times s^{2}\\&=5\times({=s})^{2}\\&={=5*s**2}\text{ cm}^{2}\end{aligned}$

Area of the four triangles (each has base ${=s}\text{ cm}$ and height equal to the slant height ${=hs}\text{ cm}$): $\begin{aligned}A_{\text{four triangles}}&=4\times\frac{1}{2}bh_{s}\\&=4\times\frac{1}{2}({=s})({=hs})\\&={=2*s*hs}\text{ cm}^{2}\end{aligned}$
Total surface area: $\begin{aligned}A_{\text{total}}&=A_{\text{five squares}}+A_{\text{four triangles}}\\&={=5*s**2}+{=2*s*hs}\\&={=5*s**2 + 2*s*hs}\text{ cm}^{2}\end{aligned}$
Therefore the total surface area of the solid is ${=5*s**2 + 2*s*hs}\text{ cm}^{2}$.
families.notes: Entry point for the surface-area half of the objective: the slant height is GIVEN (as in the book's we17), so there is no Pythagoras step, and the only decision is which faces are exposed: 5 squares + 4 triangles (the top of the cube and the pyramid's base are covered). Book model: ex13-7-20a, whose method (5 s^2 + 4 * 1/2 * b * h_s) this reuses, minus the height subtraction and the square root and rounding that make it advanced. hs is a whole number between s//2 + 2 and 1.5 s, always more than half the edge, so a real pyramid with that slant height exists; no pyramid height is mentioned, so uses-pyramid-height-for-triangular-faces cannot arise here. The likeliest wrong answer is mc:g10m13s3-2-2:counts-covered-faces (6 s^2 + 2 s hs, or also adding the pyramid's base). Numeric family, so no distractors carry the id.

families.stem: The volume of a rectangular prism is {=v} cm$^3$. The height of the prism is multiplied by a constant factor of {=k}, while its length and breadth stay the same. Calculate the volume of the new prism, in cm$^3$.
solution: The volume of a rectangular prism is given by $V=l\times b\times h$, so for the original prism $l\times b\times h={=v}$.
If the height is multiplied by a constant factor of {=k}, the new volume is $V_{\text{new}}=l\times b\times({=k}h)={=k}\times(l\times b\times h)={=k}V$.
So the volume of the prism increases by a factor of {=k}: $V_{\text{new}}={=k}\times{=v}={=k*v}$ cm$^3$.
families.notes: Entry point of the skill: ONE dimension scaled by a constant factor, so the volume is scaled by that same factor (book Ex 13.6 Q4 steps down to a single dimension). The original volume is given instead of the dimensions so the student must use the factor idea (V_new = k x V) rather than recompute from three lengths; the book's own questions are likewise abstract (no dimensions). The dimension scaled is always the height, so no instance is ambiguous. The original volume is any whole number of cm^3; no integer dimensions are implied or needed. Surface area is deliberately not asked here: with only one or two dimensions scaled the surface area is not a single constant multiple of the original, so a 'factor' only exists when all three dimensions are scaled (see the advanced family). Answer is the bare number of cm^3 (the stem names the unit).

families.stem: A rectangular prism has a surface area of {=s} cm$^2$ and a volume of {=v} cm$^3$. Its length, breadth and height are all multiplied by the same constant factor, and the volume of the new prism is {=n} cm$^3$. Calculate the surface area of the new prism, in cm$^2$.
solution: Let each of the length, breadth and height be multiplied by a constant factor of $k$, so the new dimensions are $kl$, $kb$ and $kh$.
The new volume is $V_{\text{new}}=(kl)\times(kb)\times(kh)=k^3\times l\times b\times h=k^3V$.
So $k^3=\frac{{=n}}{{=v}}={=k**3}$, which gives $k={=k}$.
The surface area of a rectangular prism is $S=2(lb+lh+bh)$, so $S_{\text{new}}=2(kl\times kb+kl\times kh+kb\times kh)=k^2\times2(lb+lh+bh)=k^2S$.
So the surface area is multiplied by a factor of $k^2={=k}^2={=k*k}$.
$S_{\text{new}}={=k*k}\times{=s}={=k*k*s}$ cm$^2$.
families.notes: Advanced: links the two factors of this objective. Book Ex 13.6 Q4b gives the all-three-dimensions case (V_new = k^3 V); here the student must run it backwards (k^3 = V_new / V, so k, a perfect cube 8, 27 or 64) and then carry k into the surface area (S_new = k^2 S, from S = 2(lb + lh + bh)). The inverse step is an extension of the book's method, not a new technique: same substitution kl, kb, kh, only the unknown has moved. The numbers are consistent by construction: l, b, h are drawn first and the stated surface area and volume are computed from them, so no impossible prism is ever shown (the student never needs l, b, h themselves). Worked check: l=2, b=3, h=4, k=2 gives S=52, V=24, new volume 192, k^3=8, k=2, new surface area 4 x 52 = 208, which equals the direct computation with sides 4, 6, 8: 2(24+32+48)=208. Largest values: new volume 8000, new surface area under 1700. Whole-number answers always, since k is an integer and S is an integer.

families.stem: The area of a rectangle is ${=A}\ \text{cm}^{2}$. Both its length and its width are multiplied by ${=k}$. What is the area of the new rectangle, in $\text{cm}^{2}$?
solution: Both dimensions of the rectangle are multiplied by the scale factor $k = {=k}$.
When every length is multiplied by $k$, the area is multiplied by $k^{2}$. So $k^{2} = {=k}^{2} = {=k ** 2}$.
$A_{\text{new}} = k^{2} \times A = {=k ** 2} \times {=A} = {=A * k ** 2}\ \text{cm}^{2}$.
families.notes: Basic entry point: one rule (area scales by k squared), whole-number enlargement, original area given, new area asked. Modelled on ex13-7-16 (square, area scales by k^2) but with a concrete area so the student applies A_new = k^2 A. Both length and width are scaled, so the rectangle is similar to the original and the k^2 rule applies. Whole-number answer always (A * k^2, at most 1000). Typical wrong answers are the catalogued errors: A * k (scale factor applied once, mc:g10m13s4-1-3:scale-factor-applied-once) and A * k^3 (wrong power, mc:g10m13s4-1-3:wrong-power-for-measure). Numeric family, so no distractor options carry those ids.

families.stem: The volume of a rectangular prism is ${=V}\ \text{cm}^{3}$. Its length, its width and its height are all multiplied by ${=k}$. What is the volume of the new prism, in $\text{cm}^{3}$?
solution: All three dimensions of the prism are multiplied by the scale factor $k = {=k}$.
When every length is multiplied by $k$, the volume is multiplied by $k^{3}$. So $k^{3} = {=k}^{3} = {=k ** 3}$.
$V_{\text{new}} = k^{3} \times V = {=k ** 3} \times {=V} = {=V * k ** 3}\ \text{cm}^{3}$.
families.notes: Basic entry point for the volume rule: whole-number enlargement of all three dimensions, original volume given, new volume asked. Parent ex13-6-5 (every side of a triangular prism quadrupled, volume scales by k^3); the figure shows a triangular prism with b, h, H, and this family uses a rectangular prism with length, width and height so that all three dimensions are named in the stem and nothing is ambiguous. Whole-number answer always (V * k^3, at most 1280). Typical wrong answers are V * k (scale-factor-applied-once) and V * k^2 (wrong-power-for-measure). Numeric family, so no distractor options carry those ids.

families.stem: A cylinder has a volume of ${=V}\ \text{cm}^{3}$. The length of its base radius and the length of its height are each made $\frac{1}{{=n}}$ of their original size. By how many $\text{cm}^{3}$ is the volume of the new cylinder smaller than the volume of the original cylinder?
solution: Both the radius and the height are multiplied by the scale factor $k = \frac{1}{{=n}}$. The shape gets smaller, so $k$ is a fraction, not {=n}.
When every length is multiplied by $k$, the volume is multiplied by $k^{3}$. So $k^{3} = \left(\frac{1}{{=n}}\right)^{3} = \frac{1}{{=n ** 3}}$.
$V_{\text{new}} = \frac{1}{{=n ** 3}} \times {=V} = {=m}\ \text{cm}^{3}$.
The volume decreases by the original volume minus the new volume: ${=V} - {=m} = {=V - m}\ \text{cm}^{3}$.
families.notes: Advanced: the book's own twist of a shrink (a unit-fraction scale factor, as in ex13-7-18 where radius and height are halved and the volume becomes 1/8) with a concrete original volume, followed by one more step (the decrease, original minus new). V is built as m * n^3 so the new volume m is always a whole number and the answer V - m is a whole number; every instance is clean. Cylinder: radius and height both scaled, so the new cylinder is similar to the original and the k^3 rule applies. The stem asks for the difference between the two volumes in unambiguous words. Typical wrong answers: reading the fraction as an enlargement (k = n, mc:g10m13s4-1-3:shrink-read-as-enlarge), V - V/n or V - V/n^2 (applied-once / wrong-power), or giving the new volume m without subtracting. Numeric family, so no distractor options carry those ids.

families.stem: The total surface area of a cone is ${=S}\ \text{cm}^{2}$. The length of its base radius and the length of its height are each made $\frac{1}{{=n}}$ of their original size. By how many $\text{cm}^{2}$ is the total surface area of the new cone smaller than the total surface area of the original cone?
solution: Both the radius and the height are multiplied by the scale factor $k = \frac{1}{{=n}}$. The cone gets smaller, so $k$ is a fraction, not {=n}.
When every length is multiplied by $k$, the surface area is multiplied by $k^{2}$. So $k^{2} = \left(\frac{1}{{=n}}\right)^{2} = \frac{1}{{=n ** 2}}$.
$A_{\text{new}} = \frac{1}{{=n ** 2}} \times {=S} = {=m}\ \text{cm}^{2}$.
The surface area decreases by the original area minus the new area: ${=S} - {=m} = {=S - m}\ \text{cm}^{2}$.
families.notes: Advanced counterpart of shrunk-volume for the area rule: the book's shrink twist (ex13-7-17, every length of a square pyramid a third, surface area scales by 1/9; ex13-6-2, the cone figure shows radius r, height H and slant height h) with a concrete original surface area and one extra step (the decrease). Radius and height of the cone are both scaled, so the slant height scales too and the cone stays similar to the original; the total surface area therefore scales by k^2. S is built as m * n^2 so the new area m and the answer S - m are whole numbers; largest S is 720. Typical wrong answers: reading the fraction as an enlargement (shrink-read-as-enlarge), S - S/n (scale-factor-applied-once), S - S/n^3 (wrong-power-for-measure), or giving the new area without subtracting. Numeric family, so no distractor options carry those ids.
